proposal: Italian Renaissance art, literature and comparative cultural inquiry

courses.name: Modern History
courses.evidence: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
courses.contribution: Modern European political and cultural transformations provide comparative context for Italian history.

courses.name: Introduction to Western Art History
courses.evidence: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
courses.contribution: Late-medieval and Renaissance painting and visual analysis provide preparation for Italian art history.

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
courses.evidence: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
courses.contribution: Close reading, narrative form and critical sources support literary analysis across genres.

courses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courses.evidence: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
courses.contribution: Behavioural and neural methods prepare students for the psycholinguistics option.

courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.evidence: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courses.contribution: Required first-year personal and professional development.

courses.name: Psycholinguistics
courses.evidence: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
courses.contribution: Experimental language processing, acquisition and bilingualism give genuine linguistic-method coverage. This is cognitive inquiry, separate from Italian grammar and dialectology.

courses.name: Great Literary Works
courses.evidence: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
courses.contribution: Comparative literary forms, including early traditions, provide interpretive tools for an Italian literature inquiry.

courses.name: Style & Meaning
courses.evidence: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
courses.contribution: Stylistic analysis of grammar, narration and discourse provides textual methods for comparison.

courses.name: History of Empires
courses.evidence: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
courses.contribution: Comparative imperial power and cultural exchange provide historical context for Mediterranean connections.

courses.name: World Myth & Literature
courses.evidence: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
courses.contribution: Ovidian retelling and comparative myth provide a specific intertextual bridge.

courses.name: Media Archaeology
courses.evidence: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
courses.contribution: Print and other media technologies support analysis of textual transmission.

courses.name: Introduction to Film & Media
courses.evidence: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
courses.contribution: Film form, history and close analysis prepare for studying national cinema.

courses.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
courses.evidence: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
courses.contribution: Italian Renaissance visual culture is a direct contribution. The course studies Italian painting, sculpture and architecture in Mediterranean and global exchange.

courses.name: Researching the “American Century”
courses.evidence: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
courses.contribution: Historical source criticism and research writing are transferable methods. The current subject is the American Century.

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.evidence: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courses.contribution: Documentary and visual qualitative inquiry provide methods for investigating cultural practices.

courses.name: Life & Travel Writing
courses.evidence: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
courses.contribution: Life and travel narratives support study of cross-cultural representation and place.

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.evidence: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
courses.contribution: Classical Roman and Greek rhetoric gives a specific historical and textual frame for argument and reception.

courses.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
courses.evidence: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
courses.contribution: Curatorial interpretation and global modern art support inquiry into heritage and display.

courses.name: Film & Text
courses.evidence: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
courses.contribution: Adaptation theory and comparative research directly support the film and literature connection. The subject is broader than Italian Neorealism.

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.evidence: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
courses.contribution: Archival and cross-cultural analysis of racial representation contributes comparative media methods. Its main context is American cultural history.

courses.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
courses.evidence: Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice. Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
courses.contribution: Poetic form, sound, close reading and performance support literary form and reception.

courses.name: Writing Art's Histories
courses.evidence: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
courses.contribution: Art-historical methods and interpretation support inquiry into visual culture across periods.

courses.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
courses.evidence: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
courses.contribution: Competing interpretive perspectives and independent textual research deepen literary analysis.

courses.name: The Documentary
courses.evidence: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
courses.contribution: Documentary history, representation and production extend cultural-film methods.

assessment: Renaissance Italy is a direct subject match. Western art, world literature, stylistics, adaptation, and independent research materially reinforce that theme. Psycholinguistics adds language processing and bilingualism. Across the full schedule, the organising substance remains comparative humanities and methods. Italian historical linguistics, dialect documentation, advanced Italian textual interpretation, translation and modern Italian society remain thin. A more language-oriented candidate would increase general language-processing methods without supplying these disciplinary objects. A film-led alternative would shift to comparative adaptation and media rather than sustain Italian literary and cultural history. No full alternative or no-match disposition is established while the comparator remains unresolved.
